Friends, Romans, countrymen. This is Mark Antony's funeral oration for Julius Caesar, a masterpiece of rhetorical manipulation in Julius Caesar. Though Caesar is dead and Antony seemingly powerless, he uses flattery, irony, and emotional appeal to turn the mob against the conspirators who murdered his leader.

Antony delivers the speech over Caesar's body in Act III, with the conspirators watching. He begins with apparent deference to Brutus and the others, calling them honourable men. He repeats this phrase with mounting sarcasm, and with each repetition it becomes a weapon. Antony catalogs Caesar's achievements and refutes the accusation that ambition drove him. Did this in Caesar seem ambitious? he asks, letting the mob answer for him.

Then Antony produces Caesar's will, promising to read it but withholding its contents, leaving the crowd desperate to know what Caesar left them. The crowd's emotional transformation unfolds before us—from accepting the conspiracy to demanding vengeance. This marks Antony's triumph and Brutus's fatal miscalculation. The speech exemplifies how language and performance can override truth, violence, and established power. It shows rhetoric at its most potent and dangerous, reshaping the will of the fickle masses and undoing the conspirators' entire political strategy.
